title: I wish I could get away with just doing 6% of my work
description:
Jensen Huang — co-founder and CEO of NVIDIA, the company whose GPUs power virtually every major AI system in the world — appeared on Cleo Abram's Huge If True podcast and explained something about the current state of visual computing that is precise enough to understand and remarkable enough to think about carefully.

NVIDIA does not render 4K images. It renders a fraction of them and uses AI to fill in everything else.

A 4K display contains approximately 8 million pixels. NVIDIA's current rendering approach — enabled by a technology called DLSS, Deep Learning Super Sampling — ray traces approximately 500,000 of those pixels. Ray tracing is the most computationally expensive method of image rendering. It simulates the actual physical behavior of light — calculating how individual light rays interact with surfaces, materials, and environments, producing reflections, shadows, subsurface scattering, and ambient occlusion with physical accuracy. Every single one of those 500,000 pixels is rendered with full physical fidelity. The result is a half-million pixels of mathematical truth.

NVIDIA then takes those 500,000 perfect pixels and provides them to an AI model trained on enormous amounts of visual data. The question the model receives: given these pixels as ground truth — given their positions, their values, the geometric and temporal context around them — what should the remaining 7.5 million pixels look like?

The AI predicts them.

And as Huang says: the image is perfect.

DLSS was first introduced in 2018. DLSS 2 arrived in 2020 with dramatically improved upscaling quality. DLSS 3 added frame generation. DLSS 4 and the Multi Frame Generation capability on RTX 50 series cards allows the AI to generate multiple predicted frames for every single rendered frame — multiplying performance while the visual quality remains indistinguishable from full rendering.

The model has been trained on enough imagery, at enough resolutions and in enough contexts, that it can accurately infer the values of pixels it has never seen based on the spatial, geometric, and temporal signals provided by the ones that were actually computed. It is not approximating randomly — it is making predictions that are, in practice, visually correct.

The broader implication Huang is articulating: AI is not an addition to the graphics pipeline. It is the graphics pipeline. The GPU computes the physical reference points that give the AI accurate information about what the scene actually looks like. The AI uses those reference points to render the visual output that the human actually sees. The division of labor — physical accuracy for a small number of computed anchors, AI inference for everything else — is the architecture NVIDIA is scaling across gaming, film production, architectural visualization, engineering simulation, and every other domain where high-fidelity imagery is required.

The GPU renders the truth. The AI fills in the world.

👉 @entrepreneursanctuary

#JensenHuang #NVIDIA #AI #Gaming #FutureTech

top_comments.author: @kingcrow15
top_comments.text:
Okay, not an expert but i think the rendered pixels move around quite a lot, so the Ai know what the render was maybe 1-4 frames ago and it knows what the surreounding correct pixels are and it guesses or interpolates the holes.

I don't know that it's perfect at doing this, but if it's making mistkes they are probably minor and then they get covered up / reset by a rendered pixel patch quickly enough that it's not very perceiveable. 

Except for a little bit of input delay, depending on how much frame gen you are doing.

Edit:
You know. I'm going to take issue with the 6% number as well, i think that's kind of like the 20% of your brain myth. As i mentioned that rendered patch probably moves around a lot so 6% can cover a lot if its moving around say 100 frames a second, it can cover 100% of pixels 6 times over.
